St. Luke of Crimea

Saints

St. Luke of Crimea

St. Luke of Simferopol · St. Valentin Felixovich Voyno-Yasenetsky · St. Luke the Surgeon

Period
1877–1961
Region
Kerch;Kyiv;Tashkent;Siberia;Simferopol
Titles / vocation
Bishop · Confessor · Physician · Writer
Commemoration
June 11

Introduction

St. Luke combined a surgical career with priesthood and episcopal service during Soviet persecution. The OCA distinguishes repeated imprisonment and exile from his later death in 1961.

Read the published life [1]

BackgroundLife and notable eventsDeath and martyrdomWritings and legacyChronology
Death / martyrdom

Reposed in1961 after surviving imprisonment and exile

Read circumstances and sources

Background

Born Valentin Voyno-Yasenetsky at Kerch, he studied art before choosing medicine and graduated from Kyiv in 1903. He married Anna Lanskaya in 1904; her death in 1919 left four children. His surgical research included a doctoral dissertation and university teaching.

[1] Official Orthodox commemoration and received life · Education,family and medical work

Life and notable events

Ordained priest in 1921, he continued medicine. He received monastic tonsure and episcopal consecration in 1923, then suffered arrests, interrogations and successive exiles. During the war he treated wounded soldiers. The OCA records the 1946 Stalin Prize for medical work and his appointment to Crimea that year.

[1] Official Orthodox commemoration and received life · Ordination,persecution and wartime work

The Church of Cyprus’s Greek account gives particular attention to his later pastoral work. It describes feeding poor people in his own home, working to reopen churches and continuing medical care without payment. The article reports the preservation of roughly750 sermons in twelve volumes and presents preaching as central to his understanding of episcopal responsibility. It also places his ministry amid renewed church closures under Khrushchev. These details are a necessary English summary of the named ecclesiastical publication, not a free-standing translation of Luke’s memoirs or an app-written instruction for worship. The source records his persistent work for the flock despite failing sight.

[2] Official Greek web commemoration;necessary English summary · Later episcopacy,sermons and renewed persecution

The Cypriot account relates the completion of his work on surgery for purulent infections during imprisonment and a long delay in publication associated with his insistence on printing his episcopal title. It also gives 1956 for final blindness, whereas the OCA gives 1958. These printed statements are kept distinct: the accounts’ biographical chronology is not silently repaired by selecting one date and presenting it as a unanimous witness.

[2] Official Greek web commemoration;necessary English summary · Imprisoned surgeon,publication and final blindness

Death and martyrdom

The OCA records complete blindness in 1958 and repose on May 29/June 11, 1961. He was buried at Simferopol. He is a confessor who survived persecution; the account does not describe a judicial execution.

[1] Official Orthodox commemoration and received life · Final illness and repose

Writings and legacy

A 2019 report on the Polish Orthodox Church records a new church dedicated to Luke at Łaźnie in the Diocese of Białystok and Gdańsk. It commemorates55 local people killed by the Nazis in 1943. Archbishop Jakub and Bishop Andrzej presided at the consecration on June 22; clergy, pilgrims and monks from Supraśl attended. A particle of Luke’s relics was placed in the altar. The report identifies it as Poland’s first church dedicated to him and thanks donors who supported its construction. This documents later veneration and a particular memorial setting, distinct from Luke’s own biography; the article’s description of the ceremony is not a newly assembled service or devotional direction.

[3] News report,July11,2019 · Łaźnie church,memorial and dedication

The OCA distinguishes local Crimean recognition in 1995–1996 from Church-wide Russian veneration in 2000.

[1] Official Orthodox commemoration and received life · Recognition and relics
